Could you tell me what the interviewer is looking for?
He hesitated before answering, and that was the best thing he did.
A genuine answer usually has one detail nobody would invent.
Community service is counted, and most applicants report almost none.
He knows the subject well, but he comes across as bored.
Where did you study?
Could you tell me where you studied?
Why did you choose that university?
I would like to know why you chose that university.
Thank you for making the time. Before we start, could you tell me how you would like me to say your name?
Gabriel is fine. May I ask whether you studied there yourself?
I did, a long time ago. That is a better first question than most people ask me. Now tell me about something you do that nobody makes you do.
I bake and sell cakes at the market in our condominium, every two weeks. I have done it for a year.
Every two weeks for a year is a commitment. Could you elaborate on the week it went wrong?
I made too many and I lost money. I wrote down what each one cost after that, and it has not happened again.
That is a genuine answer, and it has a detail nobody would invent. Do you do anything for people outside your family?
On Saturdays I help at the chapel at school. I did not know that counted as community service.
It counts, and being a volunteer for two years counts far more than being one for two weeks in the year you apply.
I was wondering what you write down about people afterwards.
Whether the person was rehearsed or thinking. You hesitated twice today and both times something real came out afterwards. I would rather read that than a perfect paragraph.
I was wondering whether you interview everybody who is shortlisted.
I would like to know why you chose your own subject.
Every two weeks for a year is a commitment, not a hobby.
Hesitating usually means somebody is actually thinking.

People ask me what makes a good interview, and they always expect me to say confidence. It is not confidence. The best conversations I have had were with candidates who hesitated, because hesitating usually means somebody is actually thinking. What I am listening for is whether the person can elaborate. I ask a small question, and a rehearsed candidate gives me the paragraph they prepared and then stops. A genuine one gives me two sentences and then keeps going, because the thing is real and there is more of it. I also notice what they ask me. If somebody has no questions at the end, I write that down, and I do not write it down as a good thing.

My interview was thirty minutes and I remember about four of them. What I remember is being asked what I do that nobody makes me do, and hearing myself talk about the food bank on Sunday mornings for far longer than I meant to. I had prepared an answer about a science prize, and I never used it. Afterwards my mother asked me whether I had asked her anything, and I had not, so I sent an email that night. I asked how she had chosen her own subject, and she wrote back a long answer. I do not know if that email changed anything. I know that it cost me ten minutes and that I would do it again.

You are shortlisted, and an email invites you to choose a time. You write back to ask whether the meeting will be online or in person. The interviewer opens by asking you to tell her about yourself. Near the end she asks whether you would like to ask her anything. You follow up the next day to thank her for her time.
